network.overall_strategy: Valine is treated as a skeleton-limited target. The network is built around the two experimentally strongest endgames: (i) Strecker capture of isobutyraldehyde to the valine aminonitrile followed by hydrolysis, and (ii) H2-driven reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate on Ni/Fe-Ni metal. Ten target-reaching pathways arise by combining two surface routes to isobutyraldehyde (reduced-gas discharge chemistry and the Patel acetone-based cyanosulfidic branch), two Strecker implementations (free HCN or ferrocyanide-released cyanide), one direct but speculative hydrothermal alpha-ketoisovalerate source, one speculative cyanide-hydrolysis bridge from isobutyraldehyde to alpha-ketoisovalerate, and two metal catalysts for the alpha-ketoacid endgame. The well-supported chemistry is concentrated in the endgames; the upstream branched-skeleton steps are kept explicit and flagged where speculative.

reactions.name: Spark/plume generation of acetone from reduced C1 gases

conditions.temperature: bulk 280-330K with transient discharge plasma hotspots
conditions.other: Reducing CH4/CO volcanic plume or atmospheric discharge; NH3 and H2O are commonly present in the full gas mixture but omitted from the net balance.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical-discharge radical chemistry generates methyl and acyl fragments that recombine to a C3 carbonyl pool; acetone is represented as a condensed product.
reactions.reasoning: CH4-bearing spark-discharge systems generate broad carbonyl pools from which higher amino acids including valine emerge after aqueous cyanide/ammonia chemistry (Ring et al., 1972; Johnson et al., 2009). This node is a balanced, product-specific compression of that radical chemistry that assigns part of the discharge carbonyl pool to acetone so the experimentally demonstrated acetone-based Patel branch can be entered; the acetone assignment is therefore weaker than the downstream cyanosulfidic chemistry and depends on locally reducing plume conditions (Johnson et al., 2008; Schlesinger and Miller, 1983).

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: HCN-bearing surface pool or stream, anoxic, neutral to mildly basic.

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic cyanide addition to the ketone forms the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) explicitly used acetone as the branch-point ketone leading into valine precursor chemistry, and cyanohydrin formation from carbonyls and HCN is the standard entry to that network. Liu et al. (2023) supports continued prebiotic access to the same cyanide/sulfur photochemical regime.

reactions.name: Hydrosulfide conversion of acetone cyanohydrin to hydroxythioamide

conditions.other: H2S/HS- rich surface water with staged sulfide delivery, anoxic.

reactions.mechanism: The nitrile sulfurizes to the corresponding alpha-hydroxythioamide under sulfide-rich conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) converted the acetone cyanohydrin into the corresponding alpha-hydroxythioamide as part of the reductive homologation sequence leading toward valine aminonitrile. This is one of the experimentally grounded substeps of the cyanosulfidic route, although the need for locally high sulfide remains a major geochemical constraint (Patel et al., 2015; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Cu/UV sulfide-driven reduction of hydroxythioamide to isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: Strong UV irradiation, anoxic, HS- supplies reducing equivalents, staged reagent delivery.

reactions.mechanism: Photoredox reduction removes the hydroxyl functionality from the alpha-hydroxythioamide and yields the higher aldehyde oxidation-state product; sulfide is oxidized to elemental sulfur.
reactions.reasoning: The Cu/UV/HS- photoredox reduction of alpha-hydroxythioamides is the key Patel-Sutherland step that accesses the isobutyraldehyde oxidation level needed for valine precursor synthesis (Patel et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2023). The equation is written in sulfide-to-elemental-sulfur bookkeeping form to keep mass balance explicit. The chemistry is experimentally grounded, but its plausibility is limited to special surface settings with strong UV and unusually high local sulfide availability (Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Spark/plume generation of isobutyraldehyde from reduced C1 gases

conditions.temperature: bulk 280-330K with transient discharge plasma hotspots
conditions.other: Reducing CH4/CO volcanic plume or atmospheric discharge; condensed products later enter surface waters.

reactions.mechanism: Radical gas-phase chain growth and carbonyl chemistry generate a branched C4 aldehyde pool that is then trapped in aqueous condensate.
reactions.reasoning: Valine is detected in classic spark-discharge products from reduced CH4-bearing gas mixtures, implying access to branched C4 carbonyl precursors before aqueous Strecker capture (Ring et al., 1972; Johnson et al., 2009). This node is therefore a balanced compression of discharge/plume product formation that assigns part of the carbonyl pool to isobutyraldehyde; that assignment is plausible but not directly isolated in the cited studies, and its global relevance depends on locally reducing atmospheres or volcanic plumes (Johnson et al., 2008; Schlesinger and Miller, 1983).

reactions.name: Classical Strecker addition to isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: Neutral to mildly basic aqueous solution with coexisting NH3 and cyanide.

reactions.mechanism: The aldehyde forms an imine with ammonia, cyanide adds to the iminium, and the alpha-aminonitrile is produced with water release.
reactions.reasoning: Catalyst-free Strecker chemistry on isobutyraldehyde is one of the best-supported valine endgames in the literature. Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013) reported valine-forming Strecker chemistry in cyanide-bearing aerosol systems, consistent with the standard aldehyde + HCN + NH3 to aminonitrile sequence. The main uncertainty is upstream aldehyde supply, not this step itself; moreover, in formaldehyde-rich mixtures the same aldehyde can also be diverted toward pantoate/pantolactone chemistry rather than valine precursors (Miller and Schlesinger, 1993; Fairchild et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Ferrocyanide-buffered aerosol Strecker addition to isobutyraldehyde
agents: ferrocyanide or Prussian Blue cyanide reservoir

conditions.other: Aerosol droplets or evaporitic films; HCN input represents releasable cyanide equivalent from ferrocyanide/Prussian Blue under UV or thermal processing.

reactions.mechanism: Released cyanide drives the same imine-then-cyanide-addition sequence as classical Strecker chemistry, but in cyanide-concentrating aerosols or evaporitic microenvironments.
reactions.reasoning: Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013) demonstrated valine-forming Strecker chemistry in aqueous aerosols using ferrocyanide or Prussian Blue as cyanide sources. This variant is important because free primitive-ocean HCN may have been too dilute for bulk Strecker chemistry, making stored and then released cyanide a more defensible geochemical scenario (Stribling and Miller, 1987; Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013).

reactions.name: Geothermal hydrolysis of valine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Geothermal heating, prolonged aqueous residence, or wet-dry cycling.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and hydrolysis convert the alpha-aminonitrile into the amino acid with ammonia release.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of alpha-aminonitriles is the established completion of Strecker chemistry. Amino-acid release only after hydrolysis is also characteristic of interstellar-ice residue studies, showing that nitrile-like precursors can persist until later aqueous heating (Muñoz Caro et al., 2002). In a prebiotic surface setting, repeated heating and hydration can complete the same conversion (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013).

reactions.name: Speculative FTT-like direct alpha-ketoisovalerate synthesis from CO and H2

conditions.other: CO- and H2-rich subseafloor hydrothermal pores, anoxic.

reactions.mechanism: Surface CO hydrogenation and C-C coupling on Fe-Ni/magnetite are taken to generate a branched C5 oxygenate pool, with alpha-ketoisovalerate represented as the target-specific alpha-ketoacid product.
reactions.reasoning: Direct abiotic synthesis of alpha-ketoisovalerate has not been demonstrated; this step is therefore explicitly speculative. It extrapolates contested Fischer-Tropsch-type CO/H2 surface chemistry on Fe-Ni/magnetite, which has been reported to generate amino acids and related organics, to the specific branched alpha-ketoacid needed for valine (Yoshino et al., 1971; Glavin et al., 2010; Elsila et al., 2021). It is included because the review identifies alpha-ketoisovalerate supply as the central unresolved bottleneck, while H2-rich hydrothermal settings remain thermodynamically favorable for amino-acid synthesis overall (Amend and Shock, 1998).

reactions.name: Speculative cyanide-hydrolysis bridge from isobutyraldehyde to alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.other: Geothermal mineral interface; net step compresses cyanohydrin formation, hydrolysis to an alpha-hydroxy acid, and dehydrogenation to the alpha-ketoacid.

reactions.mechanism: Isobutyraldehyde first equilibrates with its cyanohydrin, nitrile hydrolysis yields the corresponding alpha-hydroxy acid, and mineral-mediated dehydrogenation gives alpha-ketoisovalerate.
reactions.reasoning: No paper in the provided set directly converts isobutyraldehyde to alpha-ketoisovalerate. This reaction is therefore speculative and represents a compressed sequence of cyanohydrin formation/hydrolysis to an alpha-hydroxy acid followed by mineral-mediated dehydrogenation to the alpha-ketoacid. The proposal is chemically motivated by the well-established cyanohydrin chemistry of isobutyraldehyde (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013), the ketoacid/hydroxyacid redox pairing seen in nonenzymatic amino-acid synthesis from alpha-ketoacids (Kaur et al., 2024), and broader Fe-enabled ketoacid interconversion chemistry (Muchowska et al., 2019). It is included as a testable crossover between cyanide-first and ketoacid-first valine routes.

reactions.name: Ni-rich metal reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine

conditions.other: pH around 8, NH4+/NH3 present, anoxic; hydrothermal pore or vent-wall mineral setting.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-ketoacid forms an imine with ammonia and is then hydrogenated on a Ni-rich metal surface to the amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated H2-driven reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine at pH 8 and 22 C with Ni catalysts, with no reaction in the absence of metal. Here a geochemically plausible Ni-bearing analog to the laboratory catalyst is used. This is one of the strongest valine-specific endgames in the literature, although competing alpha-hydroxyisovalerate formation shows that the step is productive but not perfectly selective (Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Fe-Ni meteoritic-metal reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine

conditions.other: pH around 8, NH4+/NH3 present, anoxic; hydrothermal or H2-rich aqueous mineral setting.

reactions.mechanism: An imine formed from the alpha-ketoacid and ammonia is hydrogenated on Fe-Ni meteoritic metal to give valine.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) also obtained valine from alpha-ketoisovalerate using ground Aletai iron meteorite, showing that Fe-Ni meteoritic metal can catalyze the same endgame. This makes meteoritic Fe-Ni grains or analogous native Fe-Ni metal a plausible prebiotic catalyst class, though the local availability of sufficiently reactive concentrated metal remains debated (Kaur et al., 2024).

pathways.name: Acetone cyanosulfidic branch plus classical Strecker
pathways.description: Reduced-gas discharge chemistry furnishes acetone, which enters the Patel-style cyanosulfidic branch to isobutyraldehyde, then classical Strecker capture and hydrolysis yield valine.

pathways.name: Acetone cyanosulfidic branch plus ferrocyanide Strecker
pathways.description: The same acetone-to-isobutyraldehyde surface branch is coupled to a ferrocyanide-buffered aerosol Strecker implementation before aminonitrile hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Direct isobutyraldehyde source plus classical Strecker
pathways.description: A reduced-gas discharge/plume branch generates isobutyraldehyde directly, which then undergoes classical Strecker chemistry and hydrolysis to valine.

pathways.name: Direct isobutyraldehyde source plus ferrocyanide Strecker
pathways.description: Direct isobutyraldehyde formation is followed by ferrocyanide-mediated cyanide release, Strecker capture, and aminonitrile hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Direct alpha-ketoisovalerate source plus Ni amination
pathways.description: A speculative hydrothermal direct source of alpha-ketoisovalerate is completed by the experimentally supported Ni-catalyzed reductive amination endgame.

pathways.name: Direct alpha-ketoisovalerate source plus meteoritic amination
pathways.description: The same speculative direct alpha-ketoisovalerate source is completed by Fe-Ni meteoritic-metal reductive amination.

pathways.name: Acetone cyanosulfidic branch diverted into alpha-ketoisovalerate then Ni amination
pathways.description: The Patel-style aldehyde branch is redirected by a speculative cyanide-hydrolysis bridge to alpha-ketoisovalerate, then closed by Ni-catalyzed reductive amination.

pathways.name: Acetone cyanosulfidic branch diverted into alpha-ketoisovalerate then meteoritic amination
pathways.description: The same speculative aldehyde-to-ketoacid bridge is followed by Fe-Ni meteoritic-metal reductive amination.

pathways.name: Direct isobutyraldehyde source diverted into alpha-ketoisovalerate then Ni amination
pathways.description: A direct reduced-gas isobutyraldehyde source is converted by the speculative cyanide-hydrolysis bridge to alpha-ketoisovalerate, then aminated on Ni-rich metal.

pathways.name: Direct isobutyraldehyde source diverted into alpha-ketoisovalerate then meteoritic amination
pathways.description: Direct isobutyraldehyde formation is followed by the speculative aldehyde-to-ketoacid bridge and Fe-Ni meteoritic-metal reductive amination.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Best encoded route. rxn_002-rxn_004 broadly track the Patel et al. acetone-based cyanosulfidic branch, and rxn_006 plus rxn_008 give a strong Strecker-to-valine endgame. The main weakness is rxn_001, which compresses nonselective discharge/plume chemistry into a single acetone-forming step, plus rxn_004, which depends on Cu/UV/HS- staging that is only described, not explicitly represented.
suggestions: Add explicit stoichiometric coefficients for rxn_001 and rxn_008.
Encode Cu catalyst, UV irradiation, and sulfide/phosphate conditions explicitly for rxn_004.
Represent known side sinks from isobutyraldehyde, including pantoate/pantolactone chemistry and competing C5 isomer formation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Close to P1, but the ferrocyanide-buffered Strecker variant is only partially encoded because rxn_007 has the same net stoichiometry as rxn_006 and omits the ferrocyanide storage/release chemistry emphasized by Ruiz-Bermejo et al. The rest of the route is plausible but still inherits the discharge-source and cyanosulfidic staging constraints.
suggestions: Add explicit ferrocyanide or Prussian Blue species and a cyanide-release step for rxn_007.
Encode Cu catalyst, UV irradiation, and sulfide/phosphate conditions explicitly for rxn_004.
Add explicit stoichiometric coefficients for rxn_001 and rxn_008.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A coherent Miller/Strecker-style route. rxn_006 and rxn_008 are strong, but rxn_005 compresses a broad and nonselective discharge chemistry into a single isobutyraldehyde-forming step without representing competing C4 aldehydes, isomeric products, or the reducing-atmosphere caveat from the spark literature.
suggestions: Replace rxn_005 with a more explicit discharge/plume aldehyde-generation subnetwork or cite measured isobutyraldehyde formation.
Model competing norvaline and isovaline precursor formation from alternative C4 carbonyls.
Add explicit stoichiometric coefficients to rxn_005 and rxn_008.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Same strengths as P3 with the added benefit of a literature-supported ferrocyanide-buffered Strecker endgame, but rxn_007 does not explicitly model ferrocyanide storage or cyanide release. The limiting issue remains rxn_005, the poorly constrained direct origin of isobutyraldehyde from reduced C1 gases.
suggestions: Replace or unpack rxn_005 into an explicit aldehyde-forming subnetwork.
Represent ferrocyanide storage and release explicitly instead of duplicating the classical Strecker net step.
Track competing C5 amino acid isomers if this route is used for validation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Ni-catalyzed reductive amination endgame is strongly aligned with Kaur et al. 2024, but the pathway relies on rxn_009, a direct abiotic alpha-ketoisovalerate synthesis that the supplied literature explicitly treats as unsolved. As encoded, the route reaches valine only by assuming the hardest step.
suggestions: Replace rxn_009 with a literature-backed source of alpha-ketoisovalerate or mark it as an external input.
Specify the Kaur-style conditions for rxn_011, including H2 pressure, NH4HCO3 or equivalent buffering, and Ni catalyst loading.
Include alpha-hydroxyisovalerate as a competing reduction product.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Similar to P5, but with a realistic Fe-Ni meteoritic catalyst for the final amination. The bottleneck is unchanged: rxn_009 has little experimental support, so the pathway remains hypothesis-driven despite a strong final step.
suggestions: Replace rxn_009 with a defended source of alpha-ketoisovalerate or treat the ketoacid as delivered rather than synthesized in situ.
Specify meteoritic metal loading and H2/NH3 conditions for rxn_012.
Include alpha-hydroxyisovalerate as a likely side product of the final reduction chemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acetone-to-isobutyraldehyde branch is the better supported part of this route, but diversion to alpha-ketoisovalerate through rxn_010 is very weak. That bridge lacks an explicit oxidation mechanism or literature precedent, and the later move from surface photochemistry to hydrothermal Ni catalysis is not physically justified in the network.
suggestions: Replace rxn_010 with a demonstrated alpha-ketoisovalerate-forming route or split it into cyanohydrin hydrolysis plus a separately defended oxidation step.
Justify transport from a UV-lit surface setting to a hydrothermal Ni environment.
Include alpha-hydroxyisovalerate as a side product of the final amination step.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Same logic as P7 with a meteoritic metal endgame. The final amination is plausible, but rxn_010 remains the dominant weakness and the surface-to-hydrothermal transfer is still unspecified.
suggestions: Replace rxn_010 with a demonstrated alpha-ketoisovalerate source or a multi-step route with explicit oxidation chemistry.
Justify transfer from the surface cyanosulfidic setting to the meteoritic-metal hydrothermal setting.
Track alpha-hydroxyisovalerate as a likely byproduct in the final step.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route combines two under-supported skeleton-forming steps before a strong final amination. rxn_005 is an overcompressed discharge source of isobutyraldehyde, and rxn_010 is an unvalidated bridge to alpha-ketoisovalerate, so most of the uncertainty lies upstream of the otherwise sound Ni step.
suggestions: Unpack rxn_005 into explicit aldehyde-generation chemistry.
Replace rxn_010 with a defended multi-step route to alpha-ketoisovalerate.
Justify the surface-to-hydrothermal transfer and include alpha-hydroxyisovalerate byproduct tracking.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Same upstream weaknesses as P9 with a plausible Fe-Ni meteoritic amination endgame. Because both precursor-forming steps are speculative, the final catalyst choice cannot rescue the overall path.
suggestions: Unpack rxn_005 into explicit discharge/plume aldehyde chemistry.
Replace rxn_010 with a supported route to alpha-ketoisovalerate or make the oxidation chemistry explicit.
Justify environmental transfer and include expected hydroxy-acid side products.

evaluation.network_feedback: Network validity is good: the graph is connected, molecule IDs are used consistently, and the RDKit check reports 0 UNBALANCED reactions. However, rxn_001, rxn_004, rxn_005, rxn_008, rxn_009, and rxn_010 should be given explicit stoichiometric coefficients. Literature alignment is strong in its framing: the network correctly treats valine as skeleton-limited and centers the two best-supported endgames, Strecker capture of isobutyraldehyde (rxn_006/rxn_007 plus rxn_008) and metal-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate (rxn_011/rxn_012). The main weakness is exactly the bottleneck highlighted in the literature: branched-skeleton supply. rxn_005 is an overcompressed and nonselective discharge/plume summary, rxn_009 has no convincing experimental support as a direct abiotic alpha-ketoisovalerate synthesis, and rxn_010 lacks a defended oxidation or dehydrogenation mechanism and published precedent. Environmental consistency is moderate because the coarse Surface label collapses plume, UV-lit sulfide pool, and geothermal settings; rxn_004 and rxn_007 omit key condition-defining catalysts or cyanide-reservoir species; rxn_007 is stoichiometrically just a duplicate of rxn_006 as encoded; and P7-P10 do not justify surface-to-hydrothermal transfer. Best encoded pathway: P1. Overall, this is a literature-aware and connected exploratory network, but it is not approval-ready until the precursor-skeleton chemistry and environmental handoffs are made much more explicit.
